card werk-mc-keys  [decided]  STALE
Cmd+1 to Cmd+5 select a tab by position
why: The strip caps at five, so a fixed position is learnable. Stepping is not.
subtree: 1 card, 1 decided, 1 stale
STALE from #werk-mc-tabs, amended on 2026-10-09 — a direct dependency
    werk-mc-keys -> werk-mc-tabs: A child card. It refines #werk-mc-tabs.
  This card's link predates the reopen, so re-read it before: werk rederive werk-mc-keys

Cmd+1 through Cmd+5 select the chip in that position. Position, not recency: a chip that moves would make the shortcut unlearnable, so the strip must keep a stable order (insertion order, not last-touched).

That constrains #werk-mc-park. Parking the least-recently-touched tab reorders the strip. It must remove a chip and close the gap, never reshuffle the survivors.

Cmd+[ and Cmd+] step to the previous and next chip. Kept as a secondary, not the primary — see #werk-mc-keys:opt0.

The page already has a global key handler for the ask bar, so this is one more branch, not new machinery.

  -> refines         werk-mc-tabs  A tab strip of card-id chips, in the bottom control cluster
  <- alternative_to  werk-mc-keys:opt0  Cmd+[ and Cmd+] stepping only, with no positional shortcut
  <- depends_on      werk-mc-open  Shift+click forks and goes there. A plain click still navigates.
  <- depends_on      werk-mc-tabs-step-wrap  A step past the last chip goes to the first, and a step before the first goes to the last
  <- depends_on      werk-mc-park  Park an idle tab. Nothing is ever closed.
Options
  werk-mc-keys:opt0  Cmd+[ and Cmd+] stepping only, with no positional shortcut
    why not: Stepping needs you to know where you are and count. With a cap of five, a fixed position is one keypress from anywhere and needs no counting. Stepping stays as a secondary binding; it just is not the primary.

card werk-chat-stdin  [decided]
Each conversation runs in an agent process that werk starts, not in the session that hosts it
why: The host application holds the input of the session it starts, so werk cannot send that session a message. An agent process that werk starts takes its input directly, so every conversation can have a real two-way channel.
subtree: 1 card, 1 decided

A session that a host application started holds its own input, and werk has no way to write to it. So the composer cannot reach such a session. To give each conversation a real two-way channel, werk starts an agent process of its own for the conversation and writes each user turn to that process's input. The clipboard stays the way to hand text to the session the person is working in.

The process werk starts uses the same input and output setup that the host uses for its own sessions, so the setup is known to work in production. The evidence is on the source.

Example:

- Conversation B runs in an agent process that werk started.
